acrimony

/AK-ruh-moh-nee/ - the stress falls on AK · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Acrimony means bitterness and angry ill will between people.

The band's farewell tour was canceled when decades of acrimony between the two founding members finally boiled over.

Example

The merger talks collapsed on the third day, and the acrimony lingered long after: executives from the two firms refused to share an elevator, and their lawyers traded accusations in the press for months.

Acrimony is sharper than ordinary disagreement or friction — it names the bitter, personal ill will that outlasts the argument itself, souring every later dealing between the people involved.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bitterness: Bitterness is the everyday word for a soured, resentful feeling, and one person can nurse it alone for years. Acrimony is mutual and out in the open: bitterness traded between people, sharpening the words on both sides of a long dispute.

venom: Venom is hatred concentrated into a single cutting remark or look — poison delivered in one strike. Acrimony is the lasting state between people that keeps producing such strikes; a feud steeped in acrimony spits venom again and again.

spite: Spite is a petty urge to wound — keying a car, withholding a favor — and it needs no open quarrel at all. Acrimony implies a history of real, open conflict between two parties: bitterness earned across a long dispute, not small private malice.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

goodwill: friendly, cooperative feeling between people

warmth: open affection with no edge of resentment

Where it sits · how deep the bad feeling runs

friction → acrimony → animosity

friction vs. acrimony: Friction is the mild, workaday version — colleagues who rub each other the wrong way but still cooperate; it stops well short of acrimony's open bitterness.

animosity vs. acrimony: Animosity goes further than acrimony: acrimony sours the words people exchange, while animosity is settled hatred that persists even in silence.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — acri-: sharp, bitter (Latin acer, acri-)

Suffix — -mony: a state or condition (Latin -monia)

Put it together: Latin acer, acri- means 'sharp, bitter' — the same bite you taste in acrid smoke — and -monia builds abstract nouns naming a state. Acrimony is literally 'the state of being sharp': bitterness so pronounced it stings everyone in the room.

Use the root in a new word: acrid: Acrid smoke from the tire fire hung over the block all afternoon.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / written

Acrimony is a formal word for bitterness that has turned personal and mutual. In everyday speech, 'bad blood' or 'bitterness' does the job; reach for acrimony in writing about disputes — divorces, lawsuits, band breakups — where the ill will itself is the story.
